strengths: Matching gradients along an initialization-to-target tunnel is a useful attack construction. Manipulating feature visualizations without changing model architecture provides a meaningful extension of earlier fooling-circuit demonstrations.

Several experiments demonstrate manipulation with modest performance loss. For ResNet-50, target CLIP similarity increases from 0.53 to 0.68 while accuracy falls from 76.13% to 75.13%. The CLIP case increases similarity from 0.60 to 0.88 while retaining a reported assault-rifle AUROC of 1.00.
The trade-off sweeps, model-size comparisons, and target-image variations provide useful empirical insights. Repeated visualization runs quantify variability arising from stochastic FV optimization.

The motivation and illustrations are clear. Detailed experimental recipes, compute information, and an implementation link support reproducibility. Limitations, dual-use risks, and image licensing are discussed transparently.
weaknesses: The mathematical specification contains a consequential sign inconsistency. Equation (3) requires the potential in Equation (4) to be -γ/2 times the squared distance, plus C. Equation (10) likewise fits a positive squared-distance potential, making the target a minimum rather than a maximum for the positive γ values reported. This must be reconciled with the implemented activation-based loss used in both ViT settings. Even after correction, Lemma 3.1 establishes convergence only for an exactly prescribed gradient field, not for the field obtained through finite fine-tuning.

The claim of preserving internal representations exceeds the evidence. Accuracy and class AUROC do not establish preservation of activation values, other encoded concepts, or feature mechanisms. Most experiments target output neurons; in the internal-feature CLIP experiment, w=1 removes the full-layer preservation term. Figure 15 also shows substantial changes in the highest-activating natural images. Held-out representation and prediction-agreement measurements are needed to substantiate this central distinction from prior attacks.

Evidence for arbitrary-target manipulation across architectures is uneven. At the reported ViT-L/32 setting, CLIP similarity changes from 0.52 to 0.50 and LPIPS from 0.74 to 0.77, providing little quantitative support for successful targeting. Large-model experiments cover very few features, and reported uncertainty reflects repeated FV generation rather than independent attack training runs. Transfer across auditor initialization and regularization choices is also not established.

Appendix A explains methodological differences from Prox-Pulse, but there is no matched empirical comparison. Ablations comparing tunnel fitting with target-neighborhood-only fitting, and isolating the preservation components, would clarify the benefits attributable to the proposed construction.

The defense and auditing claims are stronger than their evaluation. Top-image examples and top-100 Jaccard overlap measure retrieval stability, not detection effectiveness; no detection rule or false-positive/false-negative rates are reported. Ordinary disagreement between synthetic and natural visualizations is not controlled for. Moreover, the proposed SAE–FV–attribution auditing pipeline is not actually executed, leaving the claim that discovering the poisoned behavior becomes effectively impossible unsupported.
